newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-U.S. TITLE ONLY POSSIBLE ENCORE FOR SAMPRAS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-U.S. TITLE ONLY POSSIBLE ENCORE FOR SAMPRAS.

text.p: After his unforgettable, tortuous comeback victory against Alex Corretja in the U.S. Open quarter-finals, the only possible encore for Pete Sampras is to go on and win the title.
To do that, the top-seeded defending champion must regroup mentally and recover physically from the four-hour battle he finally won in a fifth-set tiebreaker on Thursday.
Waiting to test Sampras in Saturday's semifinals is hard-serving Croatian Goran Ivanisevic, the fourth seed.
The other semifinal at the National Tennis Centre stadium is an all-American clash between second-seeded Michael Chang and sixth-seeded Andre Agassi.
An exhausted Sampras has not talked publicly since Spaniard Corretja pressed him to the point of abject fatigue and debilitating dehydration and was reported to be resting on Friday.
Those closest to the 25-year-old American are not concerned about his recuperative powers for the weekend push for his fourth Open crown.
"I'm not even worried about it," Sampras's coach Paul Annacone said. "Knowing Pete, I would say he will be ready to play on Saturday."
Annacone has coached Sampras since last year when Tim Gullikson was stricken with brain cancer. Gullikson died this year, but his twin brother Tom has never stopped applauding Sampras's effort.
"He's got a champion's reserve," said Gullikson, who has also coached Sampras as captain of the U.S. Davis Cup team.
Sampras needed every ounce of that champion's reserve in the final points to win the tiebreaker 9-7 against Corretja.
Sampras was exhausted, he had already vomitted on the court and in between points he was bent over, using his racket as a crutch to stay upright.
"He had reached the boundary and somehow he found a way to extend it and somehow he found a way to will himself to win that match," said Gullikson.
"That's all it was, it was just determination and will to win the match. At the end it really wasn't even about tennis, even though they happened to be playing tennis."
Said Annacone: "Special things happen to special people and champions can do stuff that we all only dream about."
Sampras, though, may have nightmares if Ivanisevic is on target with his rocket serves.
In five matches, Ivanisevic has collected 98 aces to reach the Open semifinals for the first time.
Sampras leads the career series 8-6, but the two have split this year's two matches. Sampras won last month in the Indianapolis final while Ivanisevic prevailed at the Lipton.

The Agassi-Chang matchup ensures a homegrown player will make it to the final for the seventh consecutive year. The match is also almost certain to be a battle of wits as well as strokes between the longtime rivals, according to Agassi.

"He has two, three, four, six, seven, eight, nine game plans that he will go to if he needs, so he can come at you with a lot of different looks," said Agassi, who beat Chang the first four times they played beginning in 1988 and leads their career series 11-6.

"I have played him where he serves 17 aces. I have played him other times where he just stays back and counterpunches and looks for me to make mistakes," said Agassi, who can reach the final for the third time in a row by duplicating his victory over Chang last month in the Cincinnati final.
"He is just a pain in the ass to be quite honest," said Agassi, the 1994 Open champion.
Chang has never reached the Open final and has not won a major since winning the 1989 French Open at the age of 17 to become the youngest men's Grand Slam champion.
If Chang does win the Open he will become the number one ranked player in the world.
